lead: A cantilever retaining wall holds back a bank of earth, for a basement, a road cut or a raised plot. It is an inverted T: a vertical stem fixed into a base slab, with the part of the slab under the retained soil called the heel and the part in front called the toe. The soil pushes the stem sideways; the soil standing on the heel holds the whole wall down. The wall is first checked as a rigid block against overturning, sliding and bearing, and only then are the stem, heel and toe designed as cantilevers. Only a few syllabi include it in this course, and walls up to about 6 m are of this type.
prereq: You need cantilever slab design (see Cantilever and continuous slabs) and the soil pressure ideas used in Wall footings.

blocks.text: For dry, level, cohesionless backfill the active pressure grows linearly with depth (Rankine): p = K<sub>a</sub>γz, with K<sub>a</sub> = (1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ), where γ is the soil unit weight and φ its angle of friction. Over the full height H, measured to the underside of the base, the thrust is P<sub>a</sub> = ½K<sub>a</sub>γH² per metre, acting at H/3 above the base.

items: Overturning about the toe: IS 456 clause 20.1 asks that 0.9 × restoring moment ≥ 1.4 × overturning moment from the earth pressure, which is a factor of safety of 1.4/0.9 ≈ 1.55. Many textbooks quote 2.0 for overturning; use what your examiner expects, and state it.

Sliding: clause 20.2 asks the same on forces: 0.9 × μΣW ≥ 1.4 × Pa, where μ is the base friction coefficient (about 0.5 for most soils). A shear key under the base adds passive resistance when this fails.
Bearing: the resultant cuts the base at x = (MR − MO)/ΣW from the toe; e = B/2 − x must not exceed B/6, and pmax = (ΣW/B)(1 + 6e/B) ≤ qs.

blocks.text: Rules of thumb fix a first trial: base width about 0.5 to 0.6H, toe about B/3, base and stem thickness about H/12 to H/10.

items: Stem: a vertical cantilever of height h (above the base) under the triangular pressure, Mu = 1.5Kaγh³/6 at its base. Main bars on the soil face, curtailed upward; distribution and nominal bars on the front face.
Heel: the soil and slab weight press down more than the soil reaction pushes up, so it bends downward from the stem: main bars at the top.
Toe: the soil pressure pushes it up: main bars at the bottom.
Shear in each part is carried by the concrete; anchor the stem bars into the base for their full development length.

examples.question: A cantilever wall is 4.5 m high from the underside of the base, with a 0.35 m base, base width 2.7 m, toe 0.9 m, and a stem 0.3 m thick at the base tapering to 0.2 m at the top (vertical back face). The backfill is level, γ = 18 kN/m³, φ = 30°, μ = 0.5, q<sub>s</sub> = 160 kN/m²; concrete weighs 25 kN/m³. Check the stability and find the stem moment.
steps: Weights per metre and their lever arms about the toe (heel 1.5 m long, stem height 4.15 m): stem, rectangular part 20.75 kN at 1.100 m = 22.82 kN·m; stem, tapered part 5.19 kN at 0.967 m = 5.01 kN·m; base slab 23.62 kN at 1.350 m = 31.89 kN·m; soil on the heel 112.05 kN at 1.950 m = 218.50 kN·m. Total ΣW = 161.61 kN/m, restoring moment M<sub>R</sub> = 278.23 kN·m/m.
Sliding: 0.9 × 0.5 × 161.6 = 72.7 kN against 1.4 × 60.75 = 85.0 kN. Not safe: friction alone gives a factor of 1.33. A shear key (or a wider heel) must supply about 13.7 kN more.

Stem: h = 4.15 m, M<sub>u</sub> = 1.5 × (1/3) × 18 × 4.15³/6 = 107.2 kN·m/m; d = 300 − 50 − 8 = 242 mm; A<sub>st</sub> = 1394 mm²/m: 16 mm bars at 140 mm c/c (1436 mm²/m) on the soil face. Shear V<sub>u</sub> = 1.5 × ½ × (1/3) × 18 × 4.15² = 77.5 kN/m, τ<sub>v</sub> = 0.320 < τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.51 N/mm².
examples.answer: Overturning and bearing pass (p<sub>max</sub> 85 kN/m², e 0.19 m); sliding fails with friction alone and needs a shear key; stem M<sub>u</sub> = 107 kN·m/m with 16 mm bars at 140 mm c/c.

traps: Putting the thrust at H/2. The pressure is triangular, so its resultant is at H/3.
Leaving out the soil on the heel. It is usually the largest stabilising weight.
Putting the heel bars at the bottom or the toe bars at the top. Heel bends down (top tension), toe bends up (bottom tension).
Using factored loads in the stability checks without the 0.9 and 1.4 of clause 20.
Taking H as the stem height in the thrust. Earth pressure acts down to the underside of the base.

quiz.q: Name the three stability checks of a retaining wall.
quiz.a: Overturning about the toe, sliding along the base, and bearing pressure under the base (with no tension, e ≤ B/6).

quiz.q: Why does the heel carry its main steel at the top?
quiz.a: The soil and slab above the heel press down more than the soil reaction pushes up, so the heel bends down from the stem like a loaded cantilever and its top face is in tension.

quiz.q: Find the active thrust on a wall of H = 5 m, γ = 17 kN/m³, K<sub>a</sub> = 0.3.
quiz.a: P<sub>a</sub> = ½ × 0.3 × 17 × 25 = 63.75 kN/m at 1.67 m above the base.

quiz.q: In the worked example, what friction coefficient would make sliding pass without a key?
The toe pressure of a wall is too high. Give two remedies and say why each works.
quiz.a: Widen the base, which lowers both the average pressure and 6e/B. Or lengthen the heel (move the stem towards the toe), which puts more soil weight behind and shifts the resultant back towards the centre, reducing e.

beyond: Not for the exam. Above about 6 m, counterfort walls, reinforced-earth walls with geogrid strips, or soil-nailed and anchored walls are cheaper than a cantilever. Drainage behind the wall (weep holes and a filter layer) prevents water pressure, which can double the thrust. Search for "counterfort retaining wall", "reinforced earth wall" and "weep holes retaining wall drainage".

figure.caption: The worked example’s cantilever wall, 4.5 m high with a 2.7 m base (toe 0.9 m, heel 1.5 m) and a stem tapering from 0.3 m to 0.2 m. The active thrust of 60.75 kN/m acts 1.5 m up on the vertical plane through the heel; the soil on the heel and the concrete hold the wall down, and the base pressure runs from 85.4 kN/m² at the toe to 34.3 kN/m² at the heel.

spec.aria: Cross-section of an inverted T retaining wall with a toe of 0.9 metres, a heel of 1.5 metres carrying the backfill, and a stem 4.5 metres high. A triangular earth pressure diagram reaching 27 kilonewtons per square metre at the base acts on a vertical line through the heel, with the resultant of 60.75 kilonewtons at 1.5 metres. Below the base, a trapezoidal pressure from 85.4 to 34.3.
